title: Choosing the Right Data Structure
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of choosing the right data structure and identify its main inputs, outputs or constraints.
Apply vector vs. list in a minimal example and state the expected result before checking it.
Test one relevant edge, missing or failure case and describe a limitation of the result.

content.intro: Choosing the Right Data Structure is part of Data Structures in R. Start with vector vs. list and connect it to the worked example and expected result.
content.why_it_matters: Choosing the Right Data Structure is one step in Data Structures in R; the shape and semantics of a data structure should match the data being represented.

content_blocks.title: Why this matters
content_blocks.text: Choosing the Right Data Structure is one step in Data Structures in R; the shape and semantics of a data structure should match the data being represented. The example is intentionally small so you can predict its result before checking it in a local R session.

items.title: Vector vs. List
items.text: Explain vector vs. list in the context of choosing the right data structure, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Matrix vs. Data Frame
items.text: Explain matrix vs. data frame in the context of choosing the right data structure, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Data Frame vs. Tibble
items.text: Explain data frame vs. tibble in the context of choosing the right data structure, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Factors vs. Character Vectors
items.text: Explain factors vs. character vectors in the context of choosing the right data structure, connect it to the example, and verify one expected result or edge case.

items.title: Dates vs. Character Strings
items.text: For dates vs. character strings, parse values to a date-time class first and verify formats, timezone assumptions and a boundary date.

items.title: Choosing Structures for Real-World Data
items.text: Compare choosing structures for real-world data using concrete trade-offs, assumptions and maintenance needs; state when each choice is appropriate.

content_blocks.title: Work through it
content_blocks.text: Preserve types during conversion and inspect dimensions, names, classes, and missing values. Change one input or condition at a time, compare the observed result with your prediction, and write down one limitation.

content_blocks.title: R example: Choosing the Right Data Structure
content_blocks.code:
# Lesson 48: Choosing the Right Data Structure
example_record <- list(id = 8, label = "sample-48", valid = TRUE)
example_record$label
content_blocks.run_instructions: CodeLeaf does not provide an R runtime. This block is an inspectable reference example; execute it in a local R console or a reviewed R-aware environment. Static validation checks file structure, not R semantics.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No example is executed by this CodeLeaf lesson. For a local run, use synthetic data in a temporary working directory, avoid production credentials or destructive writes, and restart a clean R session to clear lesson objects.
content_blocks.limitations: A list preserves named fields even when the fields have different types. Verify the snippet and expected output with the supported R and package versions before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Common pitfall
content_blocks.text: Do not treat a syntactically plausible example as proof of correctness. For choosing the right data structure, check the input type, missing/empty cases, output shape, and domain assumptions.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example without checking its inputs or output shape.
common_mistakes.why: R can coerce types, propagate missing values or simplify results unexpectedly.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect with str(), class(), typeof(), length() or dim() and add a direct check.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a demonstration as proof that every edge case works.
common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing values, dependencies and version differences can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Test a normal case and a boundary/failure case in a clean local R session.

common_mistakes.why: The conclusion depends on data provenance, transformations and assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Record input source, cleaning choices and known limitations beside the result.
